prompt: Add a follow camera with a deadzone so small player movements do not move the view.

config.plan_model: Agent-tool model parameter 'sonnet' (Claude Code sub-agent; the harness did not report the resolved model id)
config.how: one fresh general-purpose sub-agent per plan, reads a job file with project brief + the developer prompt, writes numbered plan (<=8 steps, no code) via Write; not Claude Code plan mode

plans.text:
1. Open level_01.tscn and player.tscn to confirm the Player node structure and whether a Camera2D already exists. Check the level's size and how the TileMapLayer extent is laid out.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player so it follows automatically, and make it the current camera. Confirm the Player's sprite and collision are unaffected by the new child.
3. Enable the Camera2D's drag margins (deadzone) on both axes and set the left, right, top and bottom margins to small values. Start with a modest horizontal margin and a smaller vertical one so jumps do not shake the view.
4. Set the camera's smoothing so that when the player leaves the deadzone, the view catches up gently instead of snapping.
5. Set the camera limits from the level bounds (the TileMapLayer's used rectangle) so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Check that the camera does not clash with player.gd (for example, any code that moves a camera, reads the viewport, or assumes a fixed screen) and adjust only if needed.
7. Run level_01 and test: small left-right steps, tiny jumps, running to the edges, and falling off a platform. Confirm the view stays still inside the deadzone and follows outside it.
8. Tune the margin and smoothing values based on feel, and verify the enemy scenes and level still look correct with the moving view.

1. Open level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player moves, what the level bounds are, and whether a camera already exists. Note the TileMapLayer extents so camera limits can match the level.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a separate camera node that tracks the Player) in the scene, and make it the current camera. Keep it centered on the Player's sprite.
3. Enable the Camera2D's drag margins (deadzone) horizontally and vertically, using Godot 4's drag settings so the view only moves once the player leaves the central zone. Start with a small horizontal margin and a smaller vertical one.
4. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle so the view never shows empty space beyond the level.
5. Turn on position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera eases toward the player instead of snapping when the deadzone edge is crossed.
6. Check that the camera does not inherit jitter from the CharacterBody2D's physics-step movement, and choose the correct process callback (physics vs idle) to match the player's update.
7. Run level_01.tscn and test by standing still, taking small steps, jumping, and running across the level, tuning the margin sizes and smoothing speed until small movements leave the view still.
8. Verify the enemy scenes and any UI still behave correctly with the moving view, and save the final camera settings in the Player scene.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm the Player node path, the level's pixel bounds (from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle), and how the player is spawned, so the camera is attached in the right place.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a dedicated follow node) in the scene, so it tracks the player automatically without extra follow logic in player.gd.
3. Enable the camera as current and keep position smoothing on, with a modest speed, so the view eases toward the target rather than snapping.
4. Turn on the Camera2D drag margins (the deadzone) for horizontal and vertical movement, and set the left/right/top/bottom margins to small fractions of the screen so tiny player motion stays inside the box and does not scroll the view.
5. Use a smaller vertical deadzone or a slight upward offset than the horizontal one if needed, so jumps do not constantly shift the view while the player still stays visible near the ground.
6. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's bounds so the view never shows empty space outside the level.
7. Make sure the camera works for both enemy scenes and level reloads, checking that respawning or restarting the level re-centers the camera on the player without a visible slide.
8. Run level_01.tscn and test standing still, small jitter, walking, jumping, and reaching the level edges, then tune margin and smoothing values until small movements do not move the view.

2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a dedicated follow node) in the scene tree, and make it the current camera.
3. Enable the Camera2D drag margins (the deadzone) and set horizontal and vertical margins so small movements stay inside the zone without scrolling the view.
4. Tune the deadzone size separately per axis, giving a smaller vertical margin than horizontal if jumps should not cause large view shifts.
5. Set camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle so the view never shows empty space beyond the level.
6. Add optional position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera eases once the player leaves the deadzone rather than snapping.
7. Run level_01 and test standing still, small walking steps, jumping, falling, and reaching the level edges, adjusting margins and smoothing as needed.
8. Confirm the camera works when the Player is respawned or the level is reloaded, and that the two enemy scenes are unaffected.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player is positioned and moved, and check whether any camera node already exists in the level or the Player scene.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make it the current camera.
3. Enable the Camera2D's drag margins (the deadzone) on both axes, and start with modest horizontal and vertical values so small movements stay inside the zone without shifting the view.
4. Tune the horizontal and vertical margins separately, using a smaller vertical margin if needed so jumps do not feel sluggish while keeping horizontal walking steady.
5. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the extents of the TileMapLayer in level_01.tscn so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Optionally enable position smoothing with a gentle speed so the camera glides when it does move, and confirm it does not conflict with the Player's physics movement.
7. Run level_01 and playtest: walk in place, make small steps, jump, and move toward edges, verifying the view stays still within the deadzone and follows smoothly beyond it.
8. Adjust margin and smoothing values based on playtesting, and check that both enemy scenes and any on-screen elements still behave correctly with the moving camera.

1. Inspect level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player is placed and whether any camera already exists, and note the level bounds from the TileMapLayer.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make it the current camera.
3. Enable the camera's drag margins (Godot 4 drag settings) for horizontal and vertical movement so the view only scrolls once the player leaves a central deadzone.
4. Choose deadzone sizes that suit the game, wider horizontally than vertically, so small jumps and walking nudges do not shift the view.
5. Set camera limits from the TileMapLayer's used rectangle so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Optionally enable position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera catches up gracefully once the player exits the deadzone.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player moves, how large the level is, and whether any camera already exists in the scene. Note the level's bounds from the TileMapLayer so the camera can be limited to them.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node so it follows automatically, and make sure it is the current camera for level_01.tscn.
3. Enable the Camera2D's drag margins (the deadzone) for horizontal and vertical movement, and choose margin sizes that let the player roam a small central area before the view scrolls.
4. Set different values per axis if needed, for example a wider horizontal deadzone and a smaller vertical one so jumping does not shake the view, while falling and climbing still track sensibly.
5. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the level bounds so the view never shows empty space beyond the tilemap.
6. Enable position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera eases to catch up once the player leaves the deadzone, and avoid pixel jitter by checking the project's pixel-snap and rounding settings.
7. Run level_01 and test walking in place, small hops, long jumps, and reaching each level edge, tuning the margins and smoothing values until small movements leave the view still.
8. Confirm the camera does not conflict with the enemy scenes or any other camera, and save the tuned values in the scene so they can be adjusted in the inspector later.

1. Review level_01.tscn and player.gd to confirm how the Player moves, what the level bounds are, and whether a camera already exists. Note the viewport size and the pixel scale of the TileMapLayer so camera values fit the game's look.
2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a separate node that tracks it) so it follows the player's position. Make it the current camera for level_01.

4. Turn on position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera eases to its target instead of snapping when the player exits the deadzone.
5. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) from the TileMapLayer's used area so the view never shows empty space beyond the level edges.
6. Make sure the camera does not inherit jitter from the Player's physics, for example by choosing the right process callback and checking that the Sprite2D does not shake when the camera moves.
7. Run level_01 and test standing still, small side-to-side steps, jumps, falls, and long runs, checking that tiny movements leave the view fixed and large movements scroll it smoothly.
8. Tune the margin sizes and smoothing speed based on playtesting, then save the scene and confirm both enemy scenes still behave correctly with the new view.

2. Add a Camera2D as a child of the Player node (or a separate node that tracks it) and enable it as the current camera so it follows the player automatically.

1. Open level_01.tscn and review how the Player node is placed and how the TileMapLayer extents define the playable area, so the camera's limits and starting position can be chosen correctly.
2. Add a Camera2D node as a child of the Player so it follows automatically, and enable it as the current camera.
3. Enable the Camera2D drag margins (the deadzone) on horizontal and vertical axes, starting with small values so minor player movement stays inside the window and the view holds still.
4. Choose separate horizontal and vertical margin sizes, with a smaller vertical margin or different offset so jumps do not feel sluggish or leave the player off-screen.
5. Set the camera limits (left, right, top, bottom) to match the level's TileMapLayer bounds so the view never shows empty space outside the map.
6. Optionally enable position smoothing with a modest speed so the camera eases toward the player once the deadzone is exceeded, avoiding jarring snaps.
7. Check that player.gd does not already create or reposition a camera, and remove or reconcile any existing camera logic to avoid conflicts.
8. Run level_01 and playtest walking, jumping, falling, and reaching level edges, then tune the margin and smoothing values until small movements are absorbed and larger ones scroll smoothly.
